segments.narration: Giant seven-foot geometric patterns kept appearing on Japan's seafloor. In 1995, divers off the coast of Amami Oshima discovered intricate circular ridges sculpted into the sand.
The radial troughs were symmetrical, dotted with crushed shells, and vanished within days. Marine biologists had never documented anything like them.
How could something create complex mathematical art in shifting ocean currents? Some suspected submarine testing, while others blamed unidentified underwater phenomena.
segments.visual_query: scuba divers exploring sandy ocean floor

segments.narration: In 2011, researchers finally set up 24-hour cameras. The architect wasn't a team of engineers, but a five-inch male white-spotted pufferfish.
He spent ten days flapping his fins tirelessly, crafting sand channels to shield incoming eggs from strong ocean currents.

verdicts.claim: In 1995, divers discovered symmetrical geometric circular patterns on the seafloor off Amami Oshima, Japan.
verdicts.note: The reference text supports that circular nest designs measuring 2 m (around 6.6 ft) were observed off the south coast of Amami Ōshima Island since 1995.

verdicts.claim: The circular sand patterns featured symmetrical radial ridges and crushed shells along the crests.
verdicts.note: The reference mentions ridges forming a series of mountains and grooves decorated with shells and coral, which gradually deteriorate/vanish without maintenance.

verdicts.claim: In 2011, researchers identified a five-inch white-spotted pufferfish as the creator using underwater cameras.
verdicts.note: The reference article states the fish is about 10 cm (3.9 in) and was named/discovered by researchers around 2014, but does not mention the specific year 2011 or 24-hour cameras.

verdicts.claim: Male white-spotted pufferfish spend over a week sculpting the sand structures to attract mates and protect eggs from ocean currents.
verdicts.note: The reference notes that males work for 7-9 days (more than a week straight) flapping their fins to form the circular structure to attract mates and guard eggs.
